free_tier.stated: Quoted: 'Use this form to apply for access to Datadog at no cost. We evaluate applications on a case by case basis.' The stated limits are qualitative: 'The number of hosts (or other types of compute units) and telemetry events may be limited.'

interface_detail: inferred from the tooling the provider documents; not probed
chaining: If the five-contributor bar is ever met, this is the widest observability grant because Datadog meters hosts rather than events, which suits a fleet of rented spot instances that churns hourly.

limits.value: Three team conditions exclude a solo maintainer before the money is discussed: the project must be at least a year old, have at least five regular contributors, and at least two maintainers must work for different companies.

limits_note: Three team conditions exclude a solo maintainer before the money is discussed: the project must be at least a year old, have at least five regular contributors, and at least two maintainers must work for different companies.
binding_note: Three team conditions exclude a solo maintainer before the money is discussed: the project must be at least a year old, have at least five regular contributors, and at least two maintainers must work for different companies.

evidence.proved: quoted 'Projects need to be at least 1 year old and have at least 5 regular contributors (maintainers or not). At least 2 maintainers need to work for different companies', the non-commercial and approved-licence conditions, and that the number of hosts and telemetry events 'may be limited'

notes: The clearest team gate: two maintainers employed at different companies is an institutional condition, not a paperwork one, and it is the reason a solo project cannot use this even after a year of work. No amount is published, so the value is null. Compare Sentry, which grants the same kind of plan to a single maintainer with no contributor count.
